units.title: What Makes Food Unsafe
units.blurb: Germs, chemicals and objects; time and temperature.

units.title: Time and Temperature
units.blurb: Cooking, cooling, holding, reheating and date marking, by the FDA Food Code and USDA.

units.title: People, Surfaces and Systems
units.blurb: Cross-contamination, allergens, hygiene, cleaning and sanitizing, and HACCP.

topics.title: Biological, Chemical and Physical Hazards
topics.short: Germs (bacteria, viruses, parasites), chemicals (cleaners, pesticides, allergens) and objects (glass, bone, metal) can all make food unsafe; bacteria need food, warmth, time and moisture.
topics.trouble: People think food that smells and looks fine is safe; the germs that cause illness usually don't change smell or look.

topics.title: The Temperature Danger Zone
topics.short: Bacteria grow fastest between 41°F and 135°F, the FDA Food Code's limits for restaurants; USDA tells home cooks 40°F to 140°F. Keep cold food cold and hot food hot.
topics.trouble: Learners think the two sets of numbers disagree; they come from different documents, and both tell you to keep food out of the middle.

topics.title: Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures
topics.short: Poultry 165°F; ground meat 160°F (USDA) or 155°F for 17 seconds (Food Code); whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb and fish 145°F; check with a thermometer in the thickest part.
topics.trouble: Cooks judge chicken by the color of its juices; only a thermometer tells you it reached 165°F.

topics.title: Cooling Food Safely
topics.short: The Food Code's two stages: from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F or below within 4 more hours. Shallow pans, ice baths and small portions make it work.
topics.trouble: Cooks put a full stockpot of hot soup straight in the walk-in; the middle can stay warm for many hours.

topics.title: Holding, Reheating, Labeling and Date Marking
topics.short: Hold hot food at 135°F or above and cold food at 41°F or below; reheat for hot holding to 165°F within 2 hours; label and date, and use ready-to-eat food within 7 days; first in, first out.
topics.trouble: Cooks reheat soup slowly in a steam table, which is built to hold food hot, not to heat it.

topics.title: Cross-Contamination and Storage Order
topics.short: Keep raw animal foods away from ready-to-eat food: separate boards, clean tools, and a refrigerator stored top to bottom by the temperature each food must be cooked to.
topics.trouble: People store raw chicken above the salad greens, so its juices can drip down.

topics.title: The Nine Major Food Allergens
topics.short: Milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame (added in 2023). Cooking does not remove an allergen; separate tools and honest answers do.
topics.trouble: Cooks think picking the nuts off a plate makes it safe, or that the fryer oil can be shared with a shrimp order.

topics.title: Handwashing, Gloves and Personal Hygiene
topics.short: Wash hands for at least 20 seconds before work, after raw meat, the restroom, touching your face or trash, and before gloving; gloves don't replace handwashing; sick workers stay home.
topics.trouble: Cooks put on gloves and then touch everything: raw meat, the phone, then the lettuce.

topics.title: Cleaning and Sanitizing
topics.short: Cleaning removes dirt and food; sanitizing reduces germs to safe levels on a surface that is already clean. Three-compartment sink: wash, rinse, sanitize, air-dry. Mix sanitizer by the label and check with test strips.
topics.trouble: People spray sanitizer on a dirty board; food and grease shield germs, so the surface must be cleaned first.

topics.title: HACCP: A Plan for Safe Food
topics.short: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points: seven principles that find where food could become unsafe, set limits there, check them and write it down.
topics.trouble: Learners think a critical control point is any step; it is a step where control is essential to stop a hazard, such as cooking or cooling.
